_provenance.notes: Alaska's saltwater charter industry is massive — 2,000+ permitted charter vessels operating from 50+ ports generate $800M+ in annual economic activity. Charter halibut (guided sport) is the fastest-growing segment. The charter/commercial allocation conflict for halibut is one of the most contentious ongoing fisheries policy battles: as commercial IFQ prices hit $90+/lb, sport charter operators argue they generate more economic value per fish caught than commercial harvesters. A charter halibut catch share program was implemented in 2014 after years of conflict.

charter_commercial_conflict.issue: Charter halibut allocation vs. commercial IFQ holders
charter_commercial_conflict.background: As IPHC TACs declined 2009-2013, both commercial IFQ holders and charter operators faced harvest cuts. Charter operators argued that because guided sport generates $85-130 in economic activity per pound of halibut (vs. $8-12 for commercial), they should receive a larger share of the allocation.

catch_share_program_2014.structure: Guided Angler Fish (GAF) — transfers between commercial IFQ holders and charter operators, allowing charter operators to supplement their allocation through lease/purchase from commercial fishermen
catch_share_program_2014.controversy: Commercial fishermen resent the mandatory GAF program; charter operators argue the allocation is still too small
catch_share_program_2014.economic_analysis: Charter generates $85-130/lb economic activity vs. $8-12/lb for commercial harvest (McDowell Group, 2018)
